query: Which transports can a ØMQ server bind a single socket to at once, and what does the example show?
expected_answer: A server node can bind to many endpoints using a single socket, so it accepts connections across different transports, e.g. tcp://*:5555, tcp://*:9999 and inproc://somename.
expected_facts: a server can bind to many endpoints with a single socket
accepts connections across different transports
example binds two tcp ports and an inproc endpoint

relevant_passages.quote:
A server node can bind to many endpoints (that is, a combination of protocol and 
address) and it can do this using a single socket.

query: why can't I just send a file of any size as one multipart message to save memory?
expected_answer: A message, single or multipart, must fit in memory, and multipart data does not reduce memory consumption. To send files of arbitrary size, break them into pieces and send each piece as a separate single-part message.
expected_facts: messages must fit in memory
multipart does not reduce memory consumption
break files into pieces sent as separate single-part messages

relevant_passages.quote:
A message (single or multipart) must fit in memory. If you want to send files of 
 arbitrary sizes, you should break them into pieces and send each piece as 
 separate single-part messages. Using multipart data will not reduce memory 
 consumption.

query: Does ØMQ's ipc transport work on Windows, and what is the inproc transport's bind ordering requirement?
expected_answer: The ipc transport does not yet work on Windows. For inproc, the server must issue a bind before any client issues a connect.
expected_facts: ipc does not yet work on Windows
inproc requires bind before connect

relevant_passages.quote:
It has one limitation: it does 
not yet work on Windows.
the server must issue a bind before any client issues a connect.

query: Why does Binary Star require manual recovery instead of automatic recovery to the primary server?
expected_answer: Automatic recovery creates a further 10-30 second service interruption, creates uncertainty for administrators about which server is in charge, and can leave operators analyzing an unclear interruption. So recovery is manual and can be done off-peak.
expected_facts: failover/recovery interrupts service for 10-30 seconds
automatic recovery creates uncertainty about which server is in charge
automatic recovery can leave the cause of an interruption unclear

relevant_passages.quote:
Failover creates an interruption of service to applications, possibly lasting 10-30 
seconds.

Automatic recovery creates uncertainty for system 
administrators, who can no longer be sure which server is in charge without 
double-checking.

query: What is the default failover timeout in the Binary Star example and what happens if you reduce it?
expected_answer: The failover timeout defaults to 2,000 msec. If you reduce it, the backup takes over more rapidly but may take over in cases where the primary server could have recovered.
expected_facts: default failover timeout is 2,000 msec
reducing it makes the backup take over faster
backup may take over when primary could recover

relevant_passages.quote:
In our example, the 
failover timeout value defaults to 2,000 msec. If you reduce this, the backup server will 
take over as active more rapidly but may take over in cases where the primary server 
could recover.

query: Does Binary Star replicate messages or state between the primary and backup servers?
expected_answer: The document says Binary Star does not replicate state or messages between servers: all server-side state must be recreated by applications when they fail over. Persistent messages and transactions are also not handled. It does not describe any replication mechanism.

query: How does Kafka pick the partition for a message that has a key?
expected_answer: Kafka generates a consistent hash of the key and selects the partition number by taking the hash modulo the total number of partitions in the topic, so messages with the same key always go to the same partition.
expected_facts: consistent hash of the key
hash modulo the total number of partitions in the topic
same key always goes to the same partition

relevant_passages.quote:
The simplest such scheme is to
generate a consistent hash of the key, and then select the partition number for that
message by taking the result of the hash modulo, the total number of partitions in the
topic. This assures that messages with the same key are always written to the same
partition.

query: Why do Kafka producers send messages in batches, and what do you give up by making batches bigger?
expected_answer: Batching reduces the overhead of a network roundtrip for each individual message. The tradeoff is latency versus throughput: larger batches handle more messages per unit of time, but it takes longer for an individual message to propagate.
expected_facts: a roundtrip per message would cause excessive overhead
batching reduces this overhead
larger batches give more throughput
larger batches increase latency for an individual message

relevant_passages.quote:
An indi‐
vidual roundtrip across the network for each message would result in excessive over‐
head, and collecting messages together into a batch reduces this.

Of course, this is a
tradeoff between latency and throughput: the larger the batches, the more messages
that can be handled per unit of time, but the longer it takes an individual message to
propagate.

query: Can Kafka's built-in replication copy data between two separate clusters in different datacenters?
expected_answer: No. Kafka's replication mechanisms are designed to work only within a single cluster, not between multiple clusters; the MirrorMaker tool, a consumer and producer linked together with a queue, is used to copy messages between clusters.
expected_facts: replication works only within a single cluster
MirrorMaker is used to copy between clusters
MirrorMaker is a consumer and producer linked with a queue

relevant_passages.quote:
The replica‐
tion mechanisms within the Kafka clusters are designed only to work within a single
cluster, not between multiple clusters.

At its
core, MirrorMaker is simply a Kafka consumer and producer, linked together with a
queue.

query: What happens to the producer when send() is called and the ProducerRecord has no partition specified?
expected_answer: If no partition was specified in the ProducerRecord, the partitioner chooses one for us, usually based on the ProducerRecord key.
expected_facts: partitioner chooses a partition when none is specified
choice is usually based on the ProducerRecord key

relevant_passages.quote:
If we specified a partition in the
ProducerRecord, the partitioner doesn’t do anything and simply returns the partition
we specified. If we didn’t, the partitioner will choose a partition for us, usually based
on the ProducerRecord key.

query: How can I guarantee messages are written in order even when retries happen, and what does it cost?
expected_answer: Set the in-flight requests per connection to 1, which guarantees messages are written to the broker in the order sent even when retries occur. This severely limits the producer's throughput, so only use it when order is important.
expected_facts: set max in-flight requests to 1
order is preserved even with retries
severely limits producer throughput

relevant_passages.quote:
Setting this to 1 will guarantee that messages will be written to the broker in
the order in which they were sent, even when retries occur.

This will severely limit the throughput of the producer, so only use
this when order is important.

query: Which compression codecs does the Kafka producer support for Zstandard and how well does it compress?
expected_answer: The text lists snappy, gzip, and lz4 as values for compression.type and compares snappy and gzip, but it does not mention Zstandard or its compression performance.

expected_answer: Add 'alias bond0 bonding' to /etc/modprobe.d/bonding.conf, create ifcfg-bond0 in /etc/sysconfig/network-scripts, and create an ifcfg file for each slave network card (ifcfg-eth1 and ifcfg-eth2), then bring the interface up with ifup bond0.
expected_facts: alias bond0 bonding goes in modprobe configuration
ifcfg-bond0 configures the bond0 interface
one ifcfg file per slave network card
bring up with ifup bond0

relevant_passages.quote:
We will name our bond bond0 and add this entry to modprobe so the kernel can load the
bonding module when we bring the interface up.
Next we create two files, one for each network card that we will use as slave in bond0.

bond_primary eth1
slaves are eth1 and eth2

slaves eth1 eth2

query: How do I let SWAT be reached from other computers instead of only localhost?
expected_answer: Change the only_from value in /etc/xinetd.d/swat; for example, only_from = 192.168.1.0/24 gives access to all computers in that /24 subnet.
expected_facts: edit the only_from value in /etc/xinetd.d/swat
example: only_from = 192.168.1.0/24 allows a /24 subnet

relevant_passages.quote: Change the only from value to enable swat from remote computers. This examples shows how to provide swat access to all computers in a /24 subnet.

query: What does security = share mean in smb.conf and what is the alternative mode?
expected_answer: Share mode lets clients provide a password for each share. The other way, user mode, lets the client provide a username/password combination before the server knows which share it wants to access.
expected_facts: share mode: client provides a password for each share
user mode: client provides username/password before the share is known

relevant_passages.quote: Setting the security mode to share will allow clients (smbclient, any windows, another Samba server, ...) to provide a password for each share.
The other way (called user mode) will allow the client to provide a username/password combination, before the server knows which share the client wants to access.

query: How do I configure Samba to use encrypted passwords with a tdbsam backend?
expected_answer: The document does not cover encrypted passwords or a tdbsam backend. It only shows share-level security (security = share) for the read-only file server examples.

expected_facts: RIP-1 does not supply a mask or prefix length with each route
advertisements for 193.1.1.0/27 and 193.1.1.0/24 are identical
router cannot distinguish all-0s subnet from entire network

For example, when using RIP-1which does not supply a mask or prefix
length with each route, the routing advertisements for subnet
193.1.1.0/27 and for network 193.1.1.0/24 are identical-193.1.1.0.

query: How many subnets does a /27 extended prefix on 193.1.1.0/24 give, and how many assignable hosts does each have?
expected_answer: Three extra bits give a block of eight subnets (numbered 0 through 7), and the 5 remaining host bits give 30 assignable host addresses per subnet (2^5 - 2).
expected_facts: three subnet bits yield 8 subnets
a /27 leaves 5 host bits
30 assignable host addresses per subnet because all-0s and all-1s cannot be allocated

relevant_passages.quote:
Since 8 = 23, three bits are required to enumerate the eight subnets in
the block.
relevant_passages.section: Defining the Subnet Mask / Extended Prefix Length

are 30 (25-2) assignable host addresses on each subnet.
